variables.title: Keep a café order in memory
variables.situation: A café needs to remember how many sandwiches you ordered, the price of one sandwich, and whether you want takeaway. Different kinds of values need different Java types.

steps.title: Name the information
steps.text: quantity is an int, price is a double, and takeaway is a boolean. Each variable gives one value a meaningful name.

steps.title: Calculate with those values
steps.text: Three sandwiches at Rs 40.5 each cost 3 × 40.5 = Rs 121.5.

steps.title: Update only what changed
steps.text: When you order one more sandwich, quantity becomes 4. Recalculate total to get Rs 162.0.

variables.output:
First total: 121.5
Updated total: 162.0
Takeaway: true
variables.change: Change quantity or price, then run again. Notice that total changes only when the multiplication runs again.

input-output.title: Read a ticket booking
input-output.situation: A booking screen receives a customer name and a ticket count. Scanner reads that information; println displays a confirmation. This demonstration uses fixed text as input so you can run it immediately.

steps.title: Receive the input
steps.text: The input contains Meena on one line and 3 on the next.

steps.title: Read the right types
steps.text: nextLine reads the name as text. nextInt reads the ticket count as a whole number.

steps.title: Show a useful response
steps.text: The program combines the two values into a confirmation message.

input-output.change: Change the booking text to another name and number. To read your own standard input instead, use new Scanner(System.in) and enter the two lines in Playground’s input box.

operators.title: Split a bill and check the remainder
operators.situation: Three friends split Rs 250. Whole-number division tells you what each person pays equally, and the remainder tells you what is left to cover.

steps.title: Divide into equal shares
steps.text: 250 / 3 is 83 because both operands are integers.

steps.title: Find what is left
steps.text: 250 % 3 is 1. Three payments of Rs 83 account for only Rs 249.

steps.title: Check a condition
steps.text: remainder == 0 asks whether the bill divided exactly. Here the answer is false.

operators.output:
Each pays: 83
Left over: 1
Exact split: false
operators.change: Change bill to 252 and predict the remainder. Keep friends above zero because division by zero is invalid.

conditions.title: Choose a delivery charge
conditions.situation: An online shop gives free delivery when the order is at least Rs 500. Smaller orders have a Rs 40 delivery charge. A switch also turns a delivery code into a readable label.

steps.title: Ask one yes-or-no question
steps.text: orderTotal >= 500 checks whether this order qualifies. At exactly 500, the answer is true.

steps.title: Choose just one branch
steps.text: An order of 420 follows else, setting the fee to 40.

steps.title: Translate a fixed choice
steps.text: The code S matches the Standard case in switch.

conditions.change: Try order totals 499 and 500. Then change code to E or an unknown value and follow the matching switch branch.

loops.title: Build a savings total day by day
loops.situation: You save Rs 20 each day for five days. A loop repeats the same update, while the day number tells you which repetition is happening.

steps.title: Start with zero
steps.text: total begins at 0 before the first day.

steps.title: Repeat an update
steps.text: Each iteration adds 20, so the totals are 20, 40, 60, 80, and 100.

steps.title: Stop at the right boundary
steps.text: day <= 5 includes day 5. After day becomes 6, the loop ends.

loops.change: Change the daily saving to 30, or change the number of days. Predict the final total before running.

tracing.title: Trace a prepaid wallet
tracing.situation: A wallet starts with Rs 200. You buy a bus ticket, add money, and buy lunch. A dry run records the balance after each statement instead of guessing the final answer.

steps.title: Start from the known state
steps.text: balance starts at 200.

steps.title: Apply statements in order
steps.text: Subtract 35 to get 165, then add 100 to get 265.

steps.title: Record the final change
steps.text: Subtracting 60 from 265 leaves 205. Printing intermediate balances makes the trace visible.

tracing.output:
Start: 200
Bus ticket: 165
Top up: 265
Lunch: 205
tracing.change: Change one transaction and trace each new balance on paper. Compare your trace with the printed lines.

number-problems.title: Read the digits of an order number
number-problems.situation: A shop makes a simple demonstration checksum by adding the digits of order number 4827. This is useful for learning digit extraction; it is not a secure checksum.

steps.title: Take the last digit
steps.text: 4827 % 10 gives 7, which is added to the sum.

steps.title: Remove that digit
steps.text: Integer division 4827 / 10 gives 482. Repeating this reveals 2, 8, and 4.

steps.title: Stop when no digits remain
steps.text: The final sum is 7 + 2 + 8 + 4 = 21.

number-problems.change: Try order 1005 and trace the zeros too. This version assumes a nonnegative order number.

pattern-problems.title: Print a small cinema seating plan
pattern-problems.situation: A small cinema has three rows with four seats in each row. Nested loops match this structure: the outer loop chooses the row and the inner loop prints its seats.

steps.title: Choose a row
steps.text: The outer loop runs for rows 1, 2, and 3.

steps.title: Print its seats
steps.text: The inner loop prints four [ ] symbols before it ends.

steps.title: Move to a new line
steps.text: println runs after the inner loop, so the next row starts underneath.

pattern-problems.change: Change the row and seat limits separately. Notice which change affects the height and which affects the width.

methods.title: Reuse a delivery-fee calculation
methods.situation: Two orders need the same delivery-fee rule. Putting the rule in a method avoids copying the if-else logic for every order.

steps.title: Give the method one input
steps.text: deliveryFee receives an order total through its total parameter.

steps.title: Return one result
steps.text: It returns 0 for totals of at least 500 and 40 for smaller totals.

steps.title: Call it for each order
steps.text: The same method produces 40 for 420 and 0 for 800.

methods.output:
Order A fee: 40
Order B fee: 0
methods.change: Add a call with 500. Change the free-delivery threshold in the method and observe that every call uses the updated rule.

arrays.title: Find the hottest day this week
arrays.situation: You have seven daily temperatures. An array stores them together, and one scan can find the maximum without creating a separate variable for each day.

steps.title: Store values in order
steps.text: temperatures[0] is Monday’s 30. The array keeps seven integer values.

steps.title: Keep the best value so far
steps.text: hottest starts with the first temperature. Replace it only when a larger value appears.

steps.title: Read each value once
steps.text: After visiting all seven days, hottest is 34.

arrays.change: Change one temperature to 38. This example assumes at least one day; an empty array needs a separate check before reading index 0.

strings.title: Clean a name entered in a form
strings.situation: A user types extra spaces around their name. String methods can clean the input and compare the result with another value.

steps.title: Remove outside spaces
steps.text: trim produces a new string containing Meena from the spaced input.

steps.title: Remember that strings do not change in place
steps.text: Assign the returned string to name; raw still holds the original characters.

steps.title: Compare text by content
steps.text: equalsIgnoreCase recognises MEENA as the same letters, regardless of case.

strings.change: Replace Meena with another name. Compare equals and equalsIgnoreCase when you change only the capital letters.

stringbuilder.title: Build a shopping receipt
stringbuilder.situation: A receipt grows as you add items. StringBuilder gives you one editable text buffer to which you can append each line.

steps.title: Create an empty builder
steps.text: It begins without any receipt text.

steps.title: Append pieces in order
steps.text: Append a label, a price, and a newline. Each append extends the same builder.

steps.title: Convert when you need a String
steps.text: toString gives the final receipt to print or save.

stringbuilder.change: Append another item before the total and update the total. Use a loop when the item list becomes longer.

array-problems.title: Find a student’s improvement
array-problems.situation: A student records four test scores. Comparing each score with the previous score tells you the improvement or decline between consecutive tests.

steps.title: Start at the second score
steps.text: Index 1 has a previous value at index 0. Starting at index 0 would access index -1.

steps.title: Compare neighbours
steps.text: Use scores[i] - scores[i - 1] to calculate each change.

steps.title: Interpret the sign
steps.text: A positive change means improvement; a negative change means a lower score.

array-problems.change: Try one score or two equal scores. A one-element array produces no changes because there is no pair to compare.

string-problems.title: Count a letter in a message
string-problems.situation: A small text tool counts how many times the letter a appears in banana. This turns a string problem into visiting characters and updating a counter.

steps.title: Visit each character
steps.text: charAt(i) reads one character at a valid index from 0 to length - 1.

steps.title: Test the character
steps.text: Only a matching lowercase a increments count.

steps.title: Accumulate the answer
steps.text: Matches at indices 1, 3, and 5 make the final count 3.

string-problems.change: Try Banana, an empty string, and a string without a. Decide whether your tool should treat A and a as equal.

edge-cases.title: Handle an empty shopping basket
edge-cases.situation: An average item price needs a count of items. An empty basket is a boundary case: dividing the total by zero would be invalid.

steps.title: Check the empty case first
steps.text: prices.length == 0 detects that there is nothing to average.

steps.title: Return a meaningful response
steps.text: For an empty basket, print No items instead of attempting division.

steps.title: Use the normal path for real data
steps.text: For prices 20 and 40, the sum is 60 and the average is 30.0.

edge-cases.change: Try a basket with one item and one with a zero-priced item. An empty basket and a basket containing zero are different cases.

mathematical-logic.title: Find when two buses meet again
mathematical-logic.situation: One bus arrives every 6 minutes and another every 8 minutes. If both arrive now, their next shared arrival is the least common multiple of 6 and 8.

steps.title: Find the shared factor
steps.text: The greatest common divisor is 2. Euclid’s algorithm finds it with repeated remainders.

steps.title: Use the relationship
steps.text: LCM(a, b) = a / GCD(a, b) × b for positive integers.

steps.title: Interpret the number
steps.text: 6 / 2 × 8 = 24, so both buses return together after 24 minutes.

mathematical-logic.change: Try intervals 5 and 10. For large intervals, use long to avoid overflowing int during multiplication.

oop.title: Represent two library books
oop.situation: A library book has information and behaviour: a title, a borrowed flag, and an action that marks it borrowed. A class groups these related ideas.

steps.title: Define a blueprint
steps.text: Book declares the fields and borrow method shared by all book objects.

steps.title: Create separate objects
steps.text: java and maths are two Book instances. Each has its own borrowed field.

steps.title: Change one object
steps.text: Calling java.borrow changes only the Java book. The maths book remains available.

oop.change: Borrow the maths book too, or create a third book. Notice that a method call needs an object whose state it can change.

recursion-basics.title: Count down to an event
recursion-basics.situation: A countdown says the current number, then asks a smaller countdown to do the rest. The work must reach a base case so it can stop.

steps.title: Stop at zero
steps.text: The base case prints Go! and returns without making another call.

steps.title: Make the task smaller
steps.text: For a positive number n, print n and call countdown(n - 1).

steps.title: Follow the calls
steps.text: countdown(3) leads to 3, 2, 1, and then the base case at 0.

recursion-basics.change: Try 5 and trace the calls. This version assumes n >= 0; a negative input would never reach its stopping condition.

complexity.title: Compare two ways to find a parcel
complexity.situation: Eight parcel IDs are already sorted. A linear scan may check every ID; binary search repeatedly halves the remaining candidates. Count the inspected elements for this one example.

steps.title: Check one by one
steps.text: Looking for ID 8 visits all eight elements with linear search.

steps.title: Discard half each time
steps.text: Binary search checks 4, 6, 7, and 8: four comparisons here.

steps.title: Describe growth, not milliseconds
steps.text: For n IDs, a scan is O(n), while binary search on sorted data is O(log n). Both examples use O(1) extra space.

complexity.change: Try target 1. A faster result on one input does not change worst-case complexity; describe how the work grows as n increases.

arraylist.title: Edit a shopping list
arraylist.situation: A shopping list changes size as you add and remove items. ArrayList handles the changing length while keeping the items in an ordered sequence.

steps.title: Create an empty list
steps.text: ArrayList<String> holds strings and starts with size 0.

steps.title: Add and remove items
steps.text: Add Milk, Bread, and Eggs, then remove the item whose text is Bread.

steps.title: Read the updated sequence
steps.text: Milk remains at index 0 and Eggs shifts left into index 1.

arraylist.change: Add a fourth item or remove index 0. Compare remove("Milk") with remove(0): one selects a value, the other an index.

linkedlist-api.title: Change both ends of a playlist
linkedlist-api.situation: A playlist needs an intro at the front and a closing track at the end. Java’s LinkedList exposes operations for both ends; it is a library class, separate from building nodes yourself.

steps.title: Add tracks at either end
steps.text: addFirst inserts Intro before the existing Track A. addLast appends Outro.

steps.title: Take the first track
steps.text: removeFirst returns Intro and removes it from the list.

steps.title: Inspect what remains
steps.text: The remaining order is Track A, then Outro. Random indexed access would need traversal.

linkedlist-api.change: Insert another track at the front. Before removing from an empty list, check isEmpty or use a non-throwing method such as pollFirst.

hashmap.title: Look up a product price by name
hashmap.situation: A shop maps each product name to its price. HashMap lets you ask for the price using the product name as a key instead of scanning a list of products.

steps.title: Pair keys and values
steps.text: Tea maps to 15 and Coffee maps to 25. Product names are keys; prices are values.

steps.title: Update an existing key
steps.text: Putting Tea again replaces its old value with 20; it does not create a second Tea entry.

steps.title: Handle missing keys
steps.text: getOrDefault returns -1 for Juice, which this example uses as a missing-product marker.

hashmap.change: Add Juice before looking it up. Use containsKey when a default value could be confused with a valid price.

hashset.title: Count unique event visitors
hashset.situation: The same visitor may scan their pass several times. HashSet keeps each distinct visitor ID once, making it suitable for counting unique visitors.

steps.title: Add visitor IDs
steps.text: Add A12, B34, and then A12 again.

steps.title: Let the set remove duplication
steps.text: The second A12 does not increase the size.

steps.title: Ask a membership question
steps.text: contains checks whether B34 has already visited. A set does not promise an iteration order.

hashset.change: Add C56 and try contains("D78"). Print size or specific membership results rather than relying on set order.

deque-api.title: Undo the most recent action
deque-api.situation: A drawing app needs to undo the newest action first. A Deque used as a stack follows last in, first out. ArrayDeque is a common Java implementation.

steps.title: Push actions as they happen
steps.text: Circle is pushed first, then Line is pushed above it.

steps.title: Undo the newest action
steps.text: pop removes and returns Line because it was added last.

steps.title: Look without removing
steps.text: peek returns Circle, the next action that could be undone.

deque-api.change: Push Rectangle before the pop. Check isEmpty before popping because an empty stack has no action to undo.

queue-api.title: Serve print jobs in arrival order
queue-api.situation: A printer receives Report before Invoice. A Queue follows first in, first out, so the older job is processed first.

steps.title: Join the back
steps.text: offer adds Report, then Invoice, to the queue.

steps.title: Serve the front
steps.text: poll removes and returns Report.

steps.title: Inspect the next job
steps.text: peek sees Invoice without removing it. ArrayDeque implements the Queue interface here.

queue-api.change: Add a third print job. Call poll until the queue is empty; a final poll then returns null.

priorityqueue.title: Pick the next scheduled reminder
priorityqueue.situation: Reminders are stored as minutes after midnight. A PriorityQueue<Integer> gives the smallest time first, even when reminders arrive in another order.

steps.title: Retrieve the earliest
steps.text: poll returns 480 because it has the smallest value.

steps.title: Retrieve the next earliest
steps.text: After removing 480, the next poll returns 510. Iterating a heap is not the same as sorted polling.

priorityqueue.change: Add minute 450 and predict the first result. Use repeated poll calls when you need the complete sorted order.

comparator.title: Sort names by length, then alphabetically
comparator.situation: A label screen wants shorter names first. When two names have equal length, alphabetical order breaks the tie. A Comparator expresses those rules.

steps.title: Choose the primary rule
steps.text: comparingInt(String::length) compares the number of characters.

steps.title: Define the tie-breaker
steps.text: thenComparing orders equal-length names alphabetically, placing Ali before Sam.

steps.title: Apply the rules consistently
steps.text: Jo comes first, followed by Ali, Sam, and Meena.

comparator.change: Add another three-letter name. Remove thenComparing temporarily and see why an explicit tie-breaker makes the intended order clear.

collections.title: Summarise a group of scores
collections.situation: Collections provides ready-made utilities for a Java List. You can find a maximum, count a repeated score, and sort the list without implementing each operation yourself.

steps.title: Inspect the original list
steps.text: Scores are 70, 90, 70, and 80.

steps.title: Ask useful questions
steps.text: max is 90 and frequency of 70 is 2.

steps.title: Sort when order matters
steps.text: sort modifies this list into ascending order.

collections.change: Use Collections.reverse after sorting. Remember that max needs a nonempty collection.

searching.title: Find a name on an unsorted guest list
searching.situation: A small guest list is not sorted. Linear search checks each name until it finds the requested guest, or reaches the end.

steps.title: Begin with not found
steps.text: index starts at -1, a value that is not a valid array position.

steps.title: Compare each name
steps.text: Check Ravi, Meena, and then Asha using equals.

steps.title: Stop on a match
steps.text: Asha is at index 2, so store 2 and break out of the loop.

searching.change: Search for a missing name and confirm that -1 remains. Also try the first guest to see early stopping.

sorting.title: Arrange delivery distances
sorting.situation: A courier wants to see nearby stops before distant stops. Sorting the distances reveals their order; it does not by itself solve the full route-planning problem.

steps.title: Start with unordered values
steps.text: The distances are 7, 2, 5, and 1 kilometres.

steps.title: Move the smallest remaining value forward
steps.text: Selection sort scans the unsorted part, selects its minimum, and swaps it into the next position.

steps.title: Repeat for each position
steps.text: The result is 1, 2, 5, 7. This teaching algorithm takes O(n²) time.

sorting.change: Try duplicate distances or an already sorted array. Trace where the smallest value moves on each outer-loop iteration.

binary-search.title: Find a seat in sorted booking IDs
binary-search.situation: Booking IDs 101, 105, 110, 120, and 130 are sorted. Binary search uses that ordering to eliminate half the remaining candidates after each comparison.

steps.title: Inspect the middle
steps.text: The first middle ID is 110. Since 120 is larger, the left part cannot contain it.

steps.title: Narrow the bounds
steps.text: Move low to mid + 1, keeping the possible answer inside low through high.

steps.title: Recognise the match
steps.text: The next middle ID is 120 at index 3. Stop with that index.

binary-search.change: Try 101, 130, and missing ID 115. Keep the IDs sorted; binary search is not valid on arbitrary order.

brute-force.title: Find two purchases that use a gift card
brute-force.situation: You want two distinct items costing exactly Rs 100 together. You can try every pair first, then replace that repeated search with a set of prices already seen.

steps.title: Understand the simple approach
steps.text: A pair of nested loops would check every pair of item positions.

steps.title: Reuse what you have already seen
steps.text: At price 60, ask whether 100 - 60 = 40 is in the set. It is, because the previous item cost 40.

steps.title: Improve the amount of work
steps.text: One scan with expected O(1) set lookups gives expected O(n) time and O(n) extra space, instead of O(n²) pair checks.

brute-force.change: Try prices {50, 50}. Checking before adding ensures that you use two positions instead of reusing the current item.

two-pointers.title: Choose two snacks within an exact budget
two-pointers.situation: Snack prices are already sorted: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Two pointers can find a pair totalling 60 by using one pointer at each end.

steps.title: Begin at both ends
steps.text: 10 + 50 is 60, so this pair meets the budget.

steps.title: Know how to move
steps.text: If the sum is too small, advance the left pointer. If too large, move the right pointer left.

steps.title: Keep items distinct
steps.text: The condition left < right prevents choosing the same position twice.

two-pointers.change: Try target 70 to see the left pointer move. This pointer rule relies on sorted prices.

sliding-window.title: Find the busiest three-hour period
sliding-window.situation: A shop records hourly orders: 2, 5, 1, 3, 6. You want the largest total over exactly three consecutive hours.

steps.title: Add the first window
steps.text: 2 + 5 + 1 gives 8.

steps.title: Slide without rebuilding
steps.text: Remove 2 and add 3 to get 9. Then remove 5 and add 6 to get 10.

steps.title: Keep the best total
steps.text: The largest three-hour total is 10, from the last three hours.

sliding-window.change: Try k = 2 and trace what leaves and enters each window. Keep 1 <= k <= orders.length.

prefix-sum.title: Answer a date-range spending question
prefix-sum.situation: Your daily spending is 20, 30, 10, and 40. A prefix-sum array lets you answer repeated range-total questions with one subtraction after a single setup pass.

steps.title: Store totals before each boundary
steps.text: prefix becomes [0, 20, 50, 60, 100]. prefix[i] totals the first i days.

steps.title: Use a half-open range
steps.text: Array indices 1 through 3 inclusive mean spending 30 + 10 + 40.

steps.title: Subtract the earlier total
steps.text: prefix[4] - prefix[1] = 100 - 20 = 80.

prefix-sum.change: Try left = 0 and right = 3 for the whole array. Keep left and right inside the array and left <= right.

hashing.title: Count votes by candidate
hashing.situation: Votes arrive as names. A frequency map groups equal names and counts how often each appears, without repeatedly scanning the whole vote list.

steps.title: Use the name as a key
steps.text: Each distinct candidate has one entry in the HashMap.

steps.title: Increment the frequency
steps.text: A missing name starts at 0. Add 1 for each arriving vote.

steps.title: Read the final counts
steps.text: Asha appears three times; Ravi appears twice. Hashing supports expected constant-time map operations.

hashing.change: Add a new candidate. Decide whether differences in case or surrounding spaces should represent the same candidate before counting.

problem-patterns.title: Recognise a fixed-window question
problem-patterns.situation: “What is the highest total over two consecutive days?” contains clues: the items must be adjacent and the length is fixed. Those clues suggest a sliding window.

steps.title: Name the required shape
steps.text: Consecutive means one continuous segment. Exactly two days means every candidate has length 2.

steps.title: Choose a reusable pattern
steps.text: Compute one window sum, then subtract the leaving day and add the entering day.

steps.title: Check against a tiny example
steps.text: For 4, 2, 7, 1 the candidate sums are 6, 9, and 8. The answer is 9.

problem-patterns.change: Compare “two consecutive days” with “any two days”. The second question removes adjacency, so the same window pattern no longer answers it.

linked-list.title: Build a simple chain of train coaches
linked-list.situation: Think of each coach as a node holding a label and a link to the next coach. Here you build those nodes yourself instead of using Java’s LinkedList class.

steps.title: Create individual nodes
steps.text: Each Node stores its coach name and a next reference.

steps.title: Connect the chain
steps.text: Engine.next points to A1; A1.next points to A2. A2.next stays null.

steps.title: Traverse using links
steps.text: Start at head and repeatedly follow next until null. No array index is needed.

linked-list.change: Insert a new coach after Engine. First preserve the old next reference, then reconnect both links so the rest of the train stays reachable.

stack-structure.title: Match opening and closing brackets
stack-structure.situation: An editor checks whether brackets are properly nested. The most recent opening bracket must be matched first, which is a last-in, first-out rule.

steps.title: Push each opening bracket
steps.text: For ([, the stack remembers ( and then [.

steps.title: Match the newest opening
steps.text: The closing ] must match the top [. Later, ) must match (.

steps.title: Require an empty stack at the end
steps.text: A leftover opening bracket or a mismatched closing bracket makes the text invalid.

stack-structure.change: Try ([)] and (() to expose different failures. This demonstration recognises round and square brackets only.

queue-structure.title: Build a small service-counter queue
queue-structure.situation: A service counter has room for three waiting IDs. A circular array can implement a queue without shifting every element after each customer is served.

steps.title: Track the occupied region
steps.text: front points to the next customer. size counts how many slots are used.

steps.title: Wrap around the array
steps.text: The next insertion index is (front + size) % capacity.

steps.title: Reuse freed space
steps.text: Serve 101, then add 103. The remaining service order is 102, then 103.

queue-structure.change: Add and remove enough times to wrap front back to zero. Try filling all three slots to understand the full condition.

binary-tree.title: Read a two-branch organisation chart
binary-tree.situation: A small demonstration team chart has a Lead with two direct reports: Engineering and Design. A binary tree allows at most two children per node; real organisations may need more.

steps.title: Represent the relationships
steps.text: Each node has a name plus left and right child references.

steps.title: Visit one level at a time
steps.text: A queue begins with Lead, then receives its children.

steps.title: Read the result
steps.text: Breadth-first traversal visits Lead, Engineering, and Design in level order.

binary-tree.change: Give Engineering two children and predict the level-order result. Compare it with a depth-first traversal.

bst.title: Look up a product ID in a search tree
bst.situation: Product IDs are arranged with smaller values on the left and larger values on the right. A binary search tree uses this rule to guide a lookup.

steps.title: Compare at the root
steps.text: Searching for 70 starts at 50. Since 70 is larger, go right.

steps.title: Follow only one branch
steps.text: The right child is 70, so the search succeeds without visiting 30.

steps.title: Understand the condition
steps.text: The ordering rule must hold throughout the tree. A badly unbalanced tree can still take O(n) time.

bst.change: Search for 60 and follow the path to null. Then insert 60 as the left child of 70 and search again.

heap.title: Promote the most urgent support ticket
heap.situation: Three support tickets have priority scores 20, 50, and 30. In a max-heap, every parent has at least as high a priority as its children, so the largest value reaches the root.

steps.title: Use array positions as tree links
steps.text: For parent index 0, its children are at indices 1 and 2.

steps.title: Choose the larger child
steps.text: 50 is larger than 30 and larger than the parent 20, so swap 50 with 20.

steps.title: Inspect the root
steps.text: The heap becomes [50, 20, 30]. The root is largest, but the entire array is not sorted.

heap.change: Change the root to 60. This example repairs the root when its child subtrees already satisfy the heap rule; arbitrary arrays need bottom-up heap construction.

recursion.title: Count files in nested folders
recursion.situation: A folder contains its own files and may contain smaller folders. Counting the files can be expressed as the folder’s own count plus the same calculation for every child folder.

steps.title: Define the result for one folder
steps.text: totalFiles returns that folder’s own file count plus its children’s totals.

steps.title: Recognise the base case
steps.text: A folder with no children simply returns its own count.

steps.title: Combine returned results
steps.text: Root has 2 files, Notes has 1, and Photos has 3. The returned total is 6.

recursion.change: Add a folder inside another child and trace when its count returns to its parent. This demonstration assumes an acyclic folder tree.

backtracking.title: Choose a two-person project team
backtracking.situation: From Asha, Bala, and Charu, list every possible team of two without listing the same team in reversed order. Backtracking builds a choice, explores it, then undoes it.

steps.title: Choose one person
steps.text: Add a name to the current team and explore later names only.

steps.title: Record a complete team
steps.text: When the team has two people, print it and return.

steps.title: Undo before the next choice
steps.text: Remove the last name so the next branch starts from the correct partial team.

backtracking.change: Add a fourth person. Watch how removing the last choice prevents names from leaking into another branch.

greedy.title: Fit the most meetings in one room
greedy.situation: Meetings occupy [1,3), [2,4), [3,5), and [5,7). If each meeting is equally valuable and you want the most non-overlapping meetings, choosing the earliest finishing available meeting is optimal.

steps.title: Order by finish time
steps.text: Sorting by each meeting’s end time reveals which one frees the room first.

steps.title: Accept only compatible meetings
steps.text: Choose [1,3), skip [2,4), then choose [3,5) and [5,7). Adjacent endpoints are allowed.

steps.title: Know why the rule fits
steps.text: Finishing earlier leaves at least as much room for future meetings. This rule does not solve weighted-value scheduling.

greedy.change: Add [1,7) and see why selecting the longest meeting first would be a poor strategy for maximising the number of meetings.

graphs.title: Find the fewest bus links between stops
graphs.situation: Stops A, B, C, and D are connected by bus links. Each link counts as one step, so breadth-first search can find the fewest links from A to D.

steps.title: Store neighbours for each stop
steps.text: A connects to B and C; both B and C connect to D. This example uses directed links.

steps.title: Explore by distance
steps.text: Start A at distance 0, discover B and C at distance 1, then D at distance 2.

steps.title: Visit each stop once
steps.text: The distance array also marks visited stops, preventing repeated exploration.

graphs.change: Add a direct link from A to D. BFS finds the fewest edges when all edges have equal cost; different travel times need a different shortest-path method.

dynamic-programming.title: Use the fewest vouchers to pay exactly
dynamic-programming.situation: Vouchers are worth 1, 3, or 4 credits, with unlimited copies. To pay 6 credits, choosing 4 first uses three vouchers (4 + 1 + 1), while 3 + 3 uses only two.

steps.title: Define a smaller answer
steps.text: dp[x] means the fewest vouchers that pay exactly x credits. dp[0] is 0.

steps.title: Try each possible last voucher
steps.text: For every value x, test dp[x - voucher] + 1 for each voucher that fits.

steps.title: Reuse the best smaller answers
steps.text: dp[3] is 1, so using another 3 gives dp[6] = 2. The answer is built from already solved totals.

dynamic-programming.change: Try target 8 or remove the 1-credit voucher and try target 2. The value -1 means an exact payment is impossible.
